rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midpoint temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Increase temperature one step to test selectivity at the sole unresolved pair while keeping the gradient unchanged. The current 8.30-minute last peak leaves time margin if temperature shifts retention unexpectedly.

Move beyond the apparent co-elution temperature to recover separation with reversed selectivity. A slightly shallower gradient should help protect other narrowing gaps, while the observed retention window suggests the last peak will remain under 10 minutes.

Slightly flatten the gradient at the best temperature to lift the critical resolution from 1.47 above 1.5. The current last peak at 8.60 minutes leaves room for this increase while targeting the maximum CRF of 1.0.

The shallower gradient reduced critical-pair resolution, so shorten the gradient to exploit the opposite trend. Extrapolation from the 14- and 16-minute runs suggests the critical pair may exceed 1.5 while the last peak elutes earlier.
The maximum CRF is achieved; now test a shorter gradient for faster fully resolved elution. This probes the speed limit, with particular attention to the pair currently at R = 1.59.

Retain injection 5 as the fully resolved benchmark and explore low-temperature selectivity with the faster gradient. Cooling may separate the newly limiting pair, though other pairs could become critical as elution order changes.

Return to the successful temperature and gradient duration, but raise the starting organic fraction to accelerate elution. This tests whether changing the gradient window preserves both critical separations better than shortening the gradient did.

Explore a faster, higher-temperature regime where the limiting pair may reverse elution order and regain separation. Injection 5 remains the maximum-score benchmark while this run tests an alternative route to shorter analysis time.

Shorten the gradient another step to test whether the reversed critical pair separates further beyond its crossover. Monitor neighboring pairs for compression while retaining injection 5 as the fully resolved benchmark.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction improves selectivity for the reversed critical pair without the severe compression seen with a six-minute gradient. This also probes a shorter elution window, with early-peak resolution as a key constraint.

Lower the starting organic fraction one step from injection 11 to recover early-pair resolution and ease the central compression. This tests whether the promising high-temperature window can yield full resolution substantially faster than injection 5.

Test an intermediate-low temperature with the raised starting organic fraction to explore a different selectivity regime. Cooling below 40 C may resolve the original critical pair, while this run checks whether the altered gradient window avoids new co-elutions.

Refine injection 8 by slightly reducing the gradient slope to recover its R = 1.29 limiting pair while preserving the other critical pair’s margin. This targets full resolution near the 7.60-minute benchmark rather than further broad selectivity exploration.

Reduce the slope one more grid step to bring the remaining R = 1.47 pair above 1.5. The other critical pair remains at 1.60, so this should provide an alternative maximum-score method with slightly more resolution margin and a last peak below 10 minutes.

Shorten injection 15’s gradient while adjusting the endpoint to increase its slope only slightly. The measured selectivity trends suggest both critical pairs can remain above 1.5, with earlier final elution than injection 15.

With maximum-score methods secured, test whether a steeper gradient at 40 C opens a faster selectivity window. Comparing this with injection 1 will show whether gradient slope improves the unresolved central pair without introducing new overlaps.

Shorten injection 12’s gradient to increase separation of the reversed critical pair while retaining its adequate early-peak spacing. This tests a faster candidate between the selectivity and compression limits identified in the high-temperature runs.

Shorten the programmed gradient from the best method while preserving its slope of 0.075 organic fraction per minute. Since all peaks previously eluted before this gradient would end, this should retain full resolution and the 7.60-minute elution window.

Test a slightly higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to balance the two critical separations. Nearby runs suggest this may retain the maximum CRF with more resolution margin, while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Increase the slope slightly from injection 19 to test the remaining speed margin near the best method. This smaller change than injection 6 targets earlier final elution while checking whether the R = 1.59 pair stays fully resolved.

Test a higher-temperature alternative with enough gradient shallowness to protect the temperature-sensitive central gap. Injection 4 suggests the last peak should remain below 10 minutes, while heating may improve its limiting R = 1.38 pair and yield another maximum-score method.

Test whether cooling the fast six-minute method restores its compressed central separations while retaining sufficient resolution after the temperature-dependent crossover. This is a final search for a faster fully resolved alternative; injection 5 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Shorten the best method’s programmed gradient to eight minutes while preserving its successful slope. The outlet gradient ends at 8.65 minutes, after the observed 7.60-minute last peak, so this should retain maximum CRF with a lower organic endpoint.

Use the final injection to test a slightly shallower slope than injection 15, targeting full resolution with additional margin at its tighter central gap. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes; injection 5 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-score method.
